# Existence and Uniqueness of Direct Limit of Sequence of Groups / Lemma 3

## Setting and notation

Throughout, we work in the standard setting of the theorem of which this is Lemma 3.

**The direct system.** Let $\left( G_n \right)_{n \in \N}$ be a sequence of groups, and for each
$n \in \N$ let
$$f_n : G_n \to G_{n + 1}$$
be a group homomorphism. For $m \le p$ in $\N$ define the *transition homomorphism*
$f_{m, p} : G_m \to G_p$ by
$$f_{m, m} := \operatorname{id}_{G_m}, \qquad f_{m, p} := f_{p - 1} \circ f_{p - 2} \circ \cdots \circ f_m \quad (m < p) .$$
Each $f_{m,p}$ is a group homomorphism, being a composite of group homomorphisms, and by construction

$$(\ast) \qquad f_{n, p} \circ f_{m, n} = f_{m, p} \qquad \text{for all } m \le n \le p .$$

(Indeed, for $m \le n \le p$ this is immediate from the definition by splitting the composite
$f_{p-1} \circ \cdots \circ f_m$ after the factor $f_{n-1}$; the degenerate cases $m = n$ and $n = p$
hold because $f_{m,m}$ and $f_{p,p}$ are identity mappings.)

**The direct limit.** Let
$$S := \set {\tuple {x, n} : n \in \N, \ x \in G_n}$$
be the disjoint union of the $G_n$, and let $\sim$ be the relation on $S$ given by
$$\tuple {x, m} \sim \tuple {y, n} \quad :\Longleftrightarrow \quad \exists \, p \ge \max \set {m, n} : \ \map {f_{m, p} } x = \map {f_{n, p} } y .$$
By Lemma 1, $\sim$ is an equivalence relation on $S$; we write $\eqclass {\tuple {x, n} } {}$ for the
$\sim$-class of $\tuple {x, n}$ and
$$G_\infty := S / \sim .$$
By Lemma 2, $G_\infty$ is a group under the operation
$$(\dagger) \qquad \eqclass {\tuple {x, m} } {} \cdot \eqclass {\tuple {y, n} } {} = \eqclass {\tuple {\map {f_{m, p} } x \, \map {f_{n, p} } y, \ p} } {} ,$$
where $p$ is any index with $p \ge \max \set {m, n}$ (the right-hand side is independent both of the
choice of $p$ and of the choice of representatives).

For the reader's convenience, proofs of these two facts are recalled in the Appendix; they are not
re-proved as part of Lemma 3 proper, but nothing below depends on any property of $G_\infty$ beyond
$(\dagger)$.

**The cone.** Let $H$ be a group and, for each $n \in \N$, let
$$h_n : G_n \to H$$
be a group homomorphism such that the family $\left( h_n \right)_{n \in \N}$ is *compatible* with the
direct system, i.e.
$$(\sharp) \qquad h_{n + 1} \circ f_n = h_n \qquad \text{for all } n \in \N .$$

## Statement

**Lemma 3.** The assignment
$$h_\infty : G_\infty \to H, \qquad \eqclass {\tuple {x_n, n} } {} \mapsto \map {h_n} {x_n}$$
is a well-defined mapping, and it is a group homomorphism.

## Step 0: compatibility for all transition maps

**Claim.** For all $m \le p$ in $\N$,
$$(\sharp\sharp) \qquad h_p \circ f_{m, p} = h_m .$$

*Proof.* Fix $m \in \N$ and induct on $p \ge m$.

*Base case $p = m$:* $h_m \circ f_{m, m} = h_m \circ \operatorname{id}_{G_m} = h_m$.

*Induction step:* suppose $h_p \circ f_{m, p} = h_m$ for some $p \ge m$. By $(\ast)$ with
$m \le p \le p + 1$ we have $f_{m, p + 1} = f_{p, p + 1} \circ f_{m, p} = f_p \circ f_{m, p}$, whence
$$h_{p + 1} \circ f_{m, p + 1} = h_{p + 1} \circ f_p \circ f_{m, p} \overset{(\sharp)}{=} h_p \circ f_{m, p} = h_m ,$$
using the induction hypothesis in the last step. By induction, $(\sharp\sharp)$ holds for all $p \ge m$.
$\Box$

## Step 1: $h_\infty$ is well-defined

The proposed rule assigns to a class $\eqclass {\tuple {x, n} } {} \in G_\infty$ the value
$\map {h_n} x \in H$, computed from a chosen representative $\tuple {x, n}$ of that class. To see that
this determines a mapping $G_\infty \to H$ we must check two things.

**(a) Totality.** Every element of $G_\infty$ is, by definition of a quotient set, of the form
$\eqclass {\tuple {x, n} } {}$ for some $n \in \N$ and some $x \in G_n$, and for such a representative
$\map {h_n} x$ is a well-defined element of $H$ because $h_n$ is a mapping $G_n \to H$. Hence a value
is proposed for every element of $G_\infty$, and every proposed value lies in $H$.

**(b) Independence of the representative.** Suppose
$$\tuple {x, m} \sim \tuple {y, n} , \qquad x \in G_m , \ y \in G_n .$$
By the definition of $\sim$ there exists $p \ge \max \set {m, n}$ with
$$\map {f_{m, p} } x = \map {f_{n, p} } y .$$
Applying $h_p$ to both sides of this equation in $G_p$ gives
$$\map {h_p} {\map {f_{m, p} } x} = \map {h_p} {\map {f_{n, p} } y} .$$
By Step 0 (applied once with the pair $m \le p$ and once with the pair $n \le p$), the left-hand side
equals $\map {h_m} x$ and the right-hand side equals $\map {h_n} y$. Therefore
$$\map {h_m} x = \map {h_n} y .$$

Thus any two representatives of the same class yield the same value in $H$, and together with (a) this
shows that
$$h_\infty : G_\infty \to H , \qquad \eqclass {\tuple {x_n, n} } {} \mapsto \map {h_n} {x_n}$$
is a well-defined mapping. Equivalently: $h_\infty$ is the unique mapping satisfying
$$(\flat) \qquad h_\infty \circ \iota_n = h_n \quad \text{for all } n \in \N,$$
where $\iota_n : G_n \to G_\infty$, $x \mapsto \eqclass {\tuple {x, n} } {}$, is the canonical map.

## Step 2: $h_\infty$ is a group homomorphism

Let $\alpha, \beta \in G_\infty$. Choose representatives, say $\alpha = \eqclass {\tuple {x, m} } {}$
with $x \in G_m$ and $\beta = \eqclass {\tuple {y, n} } {}$ with $y \in G_n$, and put
$p := \max \set {m, n}$, so that $m \le p$ and $n \le p$. By $(\dagger)$,
$$\alpha \beta = \eqclass {\tuple {\map {f_{m, p} } x \, \map {f_{n, p} } y, \ p} } {} .$$
Since $\map {f_{m, p} } x \, \map {f_{n, p} } y$ is an element of the group $G_p$, the displayed
expression is a legitimate representative of $\alpha\beta$ indexed by $p$, and hence, by Step 1
(which guarantees the value of $h_\infty$ may be computed from *any* representative),
$$\map {h_\infty} {\alpha \beta} = \map {h_p} {\map {f_{m, p} } x \, \map {f_{n, p} } y} .$$
Now $h_p$ is a group homomorphism, so
$$\map {h_p} {\map {f_{m, p} } x \, \map {f_{n, p} } y} = \map {h_p} {\map {f_{m, p} } x} \cdot \map {h_p} {\map {f_{n, p} } y} ,$$
and by Step 0 the two factors on the right equal $\map {h_m} x$ and $\map {h_n} y$ respectively.
Therefore
$$\map {h_\infty} {\alpha \beta} = \map {h_m} x \cdot \map {h_n} y = \map {h_\infty} \alpha \cdot \map {h_\infty} \beta ,$$
the last equality again by Step 1 (the value of $h_\infty$ at $\alpha$ resp. $\beta$ is computed from
the chosen representatives).

Since $\alpha, \beta \in G_\infty$ were arbitrary, $h_\infty$ preserves the group operation, i.e. it is
a group homomorphism from $G_\infty$ to $H$.

(As is automatic for a mapping between groups preserving the operation, $h_\infty$ also carries the
identity to the identity and inverses to inverses: $\map {h_\infty} {e_{G_\infty} }$ is idempotent in
$H$, hence equals $e_H$, and then
$\map {h_\infty} {\alpha^{-1} } \map {h_\infty} \alpha = \map {h_\infty} {e_{G_\infty} } = e_H$.)

$\blacksquare$

## Appendix: the two facts quoted from Lemmas 1 and 2

*(Included only for completeness; these are the statements of Lemma 1 and Lemma 2 of the same
theorem.)*

**Lemma 1: $\sim$ is an equivalence relation.**

*Reflexivity:* $f_{n, n} = \operatorname{id}_{G_n}$, so $\map {f_{n,n} } x = \map {f_{n,n} } x$ and
$\tuple {x, n} \sim \tuple {x, n}$ (take $p = n$).

*Symmetry:* immediate, the defining condition being symmetric in the two pairs.

*Transitivity:* suppose $\tuple {x, l} \sim \tuple {y, m}$ and $\tuple {y, m} \sim \tuple {z, n}$, say
$\map {f_{l, p} } x = \map {f_{m, p} } y$ with $p \ge \max \set {l, m}$ and
$\map {f_{m, q} } y = \map {f_{n, q} } z$ with $q \ge \max \set {m, n}$. Put $r := \max \set {p, q}$.
Using $(\ast)$ repeatedly,
$$\map {f_{l, r} } x = \map {f_{p, r} } {\map {f_{l, p} } x} = \map {f_{p, r} } {\map {f_{m, p} } y} = \map {f_{m, r} } y = \map {f_{q, r} } {\map {f_{m, q} } y} = \map {f_{q, r} } {\map {f_{n, q} } z} = \map {f_{n, r} } z ,$$
and $r \ge \max \set {l, n}$, so $\tuple {x, l} \sim \tuple {z, n}$.

**Lemma 2: $(\dagger)$ is a well-defined group operation.**

*Independence of $p$:* if $p, p' \ge \max \set {m, n}$ and $r \ge \max \set {p, p'}$, then by $(\ast)$
and the fact that $f_{p, r}$ is a homomorphism,
$$\map {f_{p, r} } {\map {f_{m, p} } x \, \map {f_{n, p} } y} = \map {f_{m, r} } x \, \map {f_{n, r} } y ,$$
and likewise with $p'$ in place of $p$; hence the two candidate representatives (indexed by $p$ and
$p'$) are both $\sim$-equivalent to $\tuple {\map {f_{m, r} } x \, \map {f_{n, r} } y, r}$, so they
are $\sim$-equivalent to each other.

*Independence of representatives:* if $\tuple {x, m} \sim \tuple {x', m'}$ and
$\tuple {y, n} \sim \tuple {y', n'}$, choose $s$ with $\map {f_{m, s} } x = \map {f_{m', s} } {x'}$
and $t$ with $\map {f_{n, t} } y = \map {f_{n', t} } {y'}$, and put $r := \max \set {s, t}$. By $(\ast)$,
$\map {f_{m, r} } x = \map {f_{m', r} } {x'}$ and $\map {f_{n, r} } y = \map {f_{n', r} } {y'}$, so
$$\map {f_{m, r} } x \, \map {f_{n, r} } y = \map {f_{m', r} } {x'} \, \map {f_{n', r} } {y'} ,$$
and by the previous paragraph $r$ may be used to compute both products. Hence the two products agree
in $G_\infty$.

*Group axioms:* associativity follows by computing all three factors at a common index $p$ and using
associativity in $G_p$; for any fixed $k \in \N$ the class $\eqclass {\tuple {e_{G_k}, k} } {}$ is an
identity (note $\map {f_{k, p} } {e_{G_k} } = e_{G_p}$ for $p \ge k$, as $f_{k,p}$ is a homomorphism,
so this class does not depend on $k$); and
$\eqclass {\tuple {x, m} } {}^{-1} = \eqclass {\tuple {x^{-1}, m} } {}$.
